title: Maximum Binary Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: recursive max-scanning per range versus a single-pass monotonic decreasing stack construction.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums with no duplicate elements, build a "maximum binary tree" recursively: the root is the maximum element in the array, its left subtree is built the same way from the subarray to the left of the maximum, and its right subtree is built the same way from the subarray to the right of the maximum. Return the root of the resulting tree.

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"The maximum in a range becomes the root, recurse on both sides\"","Classic divide-and-conquer tree construction"],["Repeatedly finding the maximum of shrinking ranges","A monotonic decreasing stack can build the same tree in a single O(n) pass, avoiding repeated max-scanning"]]}

blocks.text: The tree is defined entirely by recursively finding the maximum in the current range: it becomes the current root, and everything before it (in the original array order) forms the left subtree, everything after it forms the right subtree, recursively.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Tournament Bracket Built from Strongest to Weakest
blocks.text: Picture ranking a lineup by strength, where the strongest competitor overall becomes the "champion" (root), and everyone originally standing to their left forms one bracket, everyone to their right forms another, recursively crowning champions within each bracket.

blocks.caption: The maximum in the current range becomes root; values before and after it recursively form the two subtrees

blocks.text: Result (preorder: root, left, right, "null" for empty children): 6 3 null 2 null 1 null null 5 0 null null null. Root is 6 (the overall max); left subtree from [3,2,1], right subtree from [0,5].

Before scanning for the maximum from scratch in every recursive call, notice that as the array is processed left to right, a MONOTONIC DECREASING STACK can track exactly which elements should become ancestors of the current element, allowing the whole tree to be built in a single O(n) pass instead of O(n squared).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The direct recursive definition (find the max, split into left/right subarrays, recurse) naturally translates into a recursive function, but re-scanning for the max in every call costs O(range size) each time, O(n squared) total in the worst case (e.g., an already-sorted array).

Observation 2: Processing the array left to right and maintaining a stack of nodes in DECREASING value order mirrors exactly how "next greater element" problems are solved with a monotonic stack.

Observation 3: For each new value, pop every smaller node off the stack, making the LAST popped node become the new value's LEFT child (since it was smaller and to the value's left, everything before the current max in its range); the new value then becomes the RIGHT child of whatever remains on top of the stack (a larger, still-active ancestor to its left).

Observation 4: After all popping and attaching, push the new value onto the stack; at the end, the bottom of the stack is the overall root.

This leads to a monotonic decreasing stack, processed left to right: pop smaller values as left children of the new value, attach the new value as the right child of the remaining top (if any), then push it, building the entire tree in one O(n) pass.
Directly implement the recursive definition: find the maximum in the current range, make it the root, and recurse on the left and right subarrays.

items: For the current range, scan to find the index of the maximum value.
Create a node with that value as the current root.
Recursively build the left subtree from the range before that index, and the right subtree from the range after it.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: This is the most direct translation of the problem's recursive definition, and is fully correct.
However, scanning for the maximum from scratch in every recursive call can degrade to O(n squared) for adversarial inputs (like a sorted array).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) worst case (e.g., sorted input), O(n log n) average for random inputs.
Space: O(n) for the tree, plus O(n) recursion depth worst case.
Limitation: repeatedly re-scanning for the maximum wastes work that a monotonic stack, processed in a single left-to-right pass, can avoid entirely, achieving O(n) overall.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why repeated max-scanning is wasteful: each element only needs to be "compared away" (popped) once across the entire algorithm, not re-scanned within every recursive call's range.

The monotonic stack construction: maintaining a stack in strictly decreasing order as values are processed left to right mirrors the tree structure directly, since each element popped off the stack for a new, larger value is exactly the case where that new value should become its ancestor.

Attaching children correctly: the LAST element popped (the smallest among those popped, since the stack is decreasing) becomes the new value's LEFT child (it was the most recent, smallest element still active before the new value); the new value then becomes the RIGHT child of whatever is left on top of the stack (a larger, unpopped ancestor), if any.

The core idea: build the tree in a single pass using a monotonic decreasing stack, avoiding any repeated scanning for maxima.

Process nums left to right with a stack of tree nodes kept in decreasing order. For each new value, pop and attach smaller nodes as its left child (the last one popped becomes the left child); then attach the new node as the right child of whatever remains on top (if any); push the new node. The stack's bottom element at the end is the root.

blocks.caption: A monotonic decreasing stack builds the entire tree in one left-to-right pass

blocks.text: The monotonic decreasing stack maintains exactly the chain of "currently active ancestors" as the array is processed left to right. When a new, larger value arrives, everything smaller than it that is still on the stack must become part of its left subtree, since they appeared before it and are smaller (the LAST one popped is the deepest and most recent, correctly becoming the immediate left child). Whatever larger value remains on the stack afterward is a genuine ancestor to the left that has not yet found its right child, so the new value correctly becomes its right child. This exactly reproduces the recursive "max of range becomes root" definition, but in a single O(n) pass.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each element is pushed and popped from the stack at most once.
Space: O(n) for the stack and the resulting tree.

blocks.text: Maximum Binary Tree is a strong example of recognizing that a recursive divide-and-conquer definition can sometimes be replaced by an equivalent single-pass monotonic stack construction, avoiding repeated re-scanning.

items: Attaching the FIRST popped element (rather than the LAST popped) as the left child, which would misplace the subtree structure.
Forgetting to attach the new node as the right child of the remaining stack top, losing part of the tree.

blocks.text: Explicitly connecting this problem to the "monotonic stack for next-greater-element" family of techniques, rather than treating it as a brand-new idea, demonstrates strong pattern transfer.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid re-scanning for the maximum every time", think: monotonic decreasing stack, built in a single left-to-right pass.

Next Greater Element, using the same monotonic stack mechanics.
Any "recursive max/min defines the structure" tree-construction problem, potentially reducible to a single-pass monotonic stack.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The recursive max-scan approach runs in O(n squared) worst-case time; the monotonic stack approach runs in O(n) time, both using O(n) space.

items: Pattern: monotonic decreasing stack, replacing repeated recursive max-scanning with a single left-to-right pass.
Core Idea: pop smaller nodes as the new value's left child (last popped becomes the left child); attach the new node as the right child of the remaining stack top; push it.
Time: O(n squared) worst case for the recursive approach, O(n) for the monotonic stack approach.
Most Important Observation: a recursive "max of range" definition can sometimes be replaced by an equivalent single-pass monotonic stack construction.
Interview Difficulty: a great example connecting tree construction to the monotonic stack pattern family.
One line memory trick: pop smaller as left child, attach to remaining top as its right child, push.
